title: You Probably Forget How Cheap Memory Used To Be – And Is Not So Now
gist: Hyperscaler AI capex is colliding with shared DRAM/NAND/HBM manufacturing capacity to push spot memory prices up roughly 7x, handing pricing power to commodity memory makers, letting Broadcom challenge Nvidia's historical control of HBM allocation, and pushing Nvidia toward a 15% price increase on its next-gen systems while the industry races toward in-memory compute (PIM) to work around the bottleneck.

insights.claim: DRAM, NAND flash, and HBM prices are surging together because all three are produced on the same manufacturing lines, so a demand shock in any one segment tightens supply and raises prices across all of them, according to Objective Analysis general director Jim Handy at Hot Chips 2026.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Because these memory types share fabrication capacity, a shortage in one (e.g. HBM for AI accelerators) mechanically tightens supply and raises prices for the others (commodity DDR, NAND) — a key causal link for anyone modeling memory-cost pass-through across the whole compute stack, not just AI GPUs.
insights.quote: It's all made on the same manufacturing line... And so because of that, it's causing DDR prices to go crazy, and all of NAND flash prices are going crazy
insights.locator: Jim Handy quote at Hot Chips

insights.claim: Spot pricing for DRAM, NAND, and HBM has risen roughly seven times, per data presented by Jim Handy at Hot Chips 2026, though spot pricing is described as an imperfect but easily measurable indicator since large buyers negotiate their own volume/price deals separately.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A 7x spot price increase is an extreme move for a historically commoditized product category, signaling the AI-driven memory shortage is a structurally large event, not a minor cyclical uptick.
insights.quote: you've got these prices that have gone up about seven times on the spot market, which is not a very good indicator, but it's an easy one to measure
insights.locator: Jim Handy quote at Hot Chips

insights.claim: Because DRAM and NAND flash are commodities where buyers care primarily about price rather than manufacturer identity, memory suppliers gain full pricing power during a shortage and can drop existing customers (even reliable payers) in favor of buyers willing to pay more.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Commodity dynamics amplify shortage-driven price spikes and mean buyers without long-term supply agreements are most exposed to being deprioritized by memory suppliers chasing higher bidders.
insights.quote: when there's a shortage, then they don't care about you... we can get a higher price from that guy over there
insights.locator: Jim Handy quote at Hot Chips

themes.theme: Hyperscaler capex as the demand driver

insights.claim: The memory boom is driven primarily by hyperscalers and cloud builders investing to be the platforms for training and inference of ever more powerful GenAI models, plus the rise of agentic AI, which requires large numbers of CPUs and substantial DRAM/flash to create sandboxes running generated Python code and other agent-executed programs.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Identifies two distinct, compounding demand vectors for memory: model training/inference (HBM/GPU-driven) and agentic AI sandboxing (CPU/DRAM/flash-driven) — both need to slow simultaneously for memory demand pressure to ease.
insights.quote: This is driving the HBM and GPU/XPU booms, as well as the ancillary DRAM and flash booms. And the rise of agentic AI, which needs tons of CPUs as well as some DRAM and flash

insights.claim: In hyperscaler AI capex data from 2021 through Q2 2026, Alibaba's spending barely registers against the 'big four' US tech titans — Amazon Web Services, Google, Microsoft Azure, and Meta Platforms — showing the AI infrastructure buildout driving memory prices is overwhelmingly a US hyperscaler phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The memory price shock is concentrated in US hyperscaler capex, meaning the trajectory of these four companies' AI investment plans is the single most important variable for forecasting memory prices, more so than Chinese demand.
insights.quote: Alibaba, the biggest of the Chinese hyperscalers that also has a cloud business, barely registers against the vast spending by the big four tech titans in the United States

insights.claim: Apple's capital investment in AI is smaller in 2026 than in each of the prior five years, making it 'barely a line' in the hyperscaler capex chart, because Apple deploys AI without building the underlying training infrastructure itself.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Apple is positioned as a capital-light free-rider on the AI infrastructure boom, monetizing AI without bearing the capex and memory-price exposure that AWS, Google, Microsoft, and Meta are absorbing — a distinct competitive/capital-efficiency angle relevant to comparing these companies' AI-related margin exposure.
insights.quote: Apple, which uses AI but does not create it, is barely a line, and in fact, its capital investments in AI are smaller in 2026 than they were for the prior five years.

insights.claim: Memory and flash maker revenues crashed in late 2022 and early 2023, right as the GenAI boom was just beginning, establishing that the current memory supercycle is a distinctly post-ChatGPT-era phenomenon rather than a continuation of a prior upcycle.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Dates the start of the current memory pricing cycle to the GenAI boom specifically, useful for separating structural AI-driven demand from any prior semiconductor cycle when modeling future memory revenue trends.
insights.quote: Look at that memory and flash crash back in late 2022 and in early 2023, when GenAI ironically was just getting started.

insights.claim: Industry prognostications reviewed by the author suggest the GenAI boom, and associated memory shortages, will continue growing at least through 2030, though the author cautions this does not mean memory revenues will rise linearly even within that structural uptrend.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A multi-year (through-2030) demand horizon for memory supports a longer investment thesis for memory makers, but investors should still expect cyclicality/volatility within that broader uptrend.
insights.quote: If the GenAI boom keeps going – and all the prognostications I have seen see it growing through 2030 at the least and shortages continuing until that time at least – then there is no reason to believe that revenues will keep going up and to the right at a linear rate.

themes.theme: Nvidia's HBM position and pricing power

insights.claim: Nvidia has historically controlled HBM memory pricing as its highest-volume buyer during the deep learning and early AI boom era, but Broadcom has now become the third-largest HBM buyer (behind Nvidia and AMD) through its custom XPU business, giving it the financial firepower to compete for HBM capacity that smaller AI hardware startups cannot access without partners like Broadcom or Marvell.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Broadcom's rise as the third-largest HBM buyer signals a real shift in bargaining power away from Nvidia's historical near-monopoly on HBM allocation, and highlights a structural bottleneck for independent AI chip startups that lack a Broadcom/Marvell-scale ASIC partner to secure memory supply.
insights.quote: Broadcom is now the third largest buyer of HBM memory, behind Nvidia and AMD, and it has the financial firepower to compete for HBM capacity

insights.claim: Nvidia is warning customers of a 15% price increase on its 'Grace-Blackwell' and 'Vera-Rubin' NVL72 systems for next year, per Bloomberg reports, with GPU components already sold out for 2026 and component allocation almost certainly locked through the end of 2027.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A concrete, near-term (15%) price increase and multi-year sold-out allocation are directly relevant to any model of Nvidia's 2026-2027 revenue and margin trajectory, and to hyperscaler capex planning that depends on Nvidia system pricing.
insights.quote: Nvidia is warning customers who are buying "Grace-Blackwell" and "Vera-Rubin" NVL72 systems next year that there is a 15 percent price increase coming, according to reports in Bloomberg.

insights.claim: The author infers Nvidia has built flexible pricing provisions into its contracts to pass rising HBM, DRAM, and flash costs through to its ODM and OEM customers, who in turn pass those costs on to end system buyers, protecting Nvidia's own margins from the memory price spike.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: If accurate, this means the memory cost spike cascades down the AI hardware supply chain to end buyers rather than compressing Nvidia's margins — relevant to evaluating Nvidia's earnings resilience versus its customers' cost exposure.
insights.quote: I assume Nvidia has put flexible pricing provisions into its contracts so it can pass through rising HBM, DRAM, and flash costs on to its ODM and OEM customers, who will in turn pass it on to the actual system buyers.

insights.claim: The article notes the US Department of Justice has historically used roughly 85% revenue or shipment market share as its threshold for calling a business a monopoly, but suggests that what actually matters today is what President Trump thinks about a company's business at any given moment.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A pointed, skeptical read that antitrust risk for Nvidia's HBM/GPU dominance is now more a function of political discretion than rules-based enforcement — worth weighing when assessing regulatory tail risk for Nvidia.
insights.quote: these days, what really matters is what President Trump thinks about your business at any given moment.

insights.claim: The industry is responding to the memory bottleneck with externalized flash-based, DPU-driven storage tiers for KV caches, and with Processing-In-Memory (PIM) — adding compute directly to HBM base dies and memory subsystems — as ways to get past the 'memory wall.'
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: PIM and KV-cache-tiered flash storage are emerging architectural responses to memory scarcity that could reduce reliance on raw HBM capacity growth — worth tracking as a potential relief valve on memory demand and pricing.
insights.quote: we are seeing that with externalized flash-based, DPU-driven storage tiers for KV caches as well as adding compute to HBM base dies and also adding compute into memory subsystems – so-called Processing In Memory, or PIM

insights.claim: Jim Handy's mental model is that the bandwidth requirement of a communications channel is inversely proportional to the intelligence at either end of it, meaning smarter memory chips that can perform operations like sorting internally reduce the amount of data traffic that needs to reach the processor.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: This bandwidth-intelligence tradeoff is a reusable mental model for evaluating any in-memory or near-memory compute architecture proposal — the more local intelligence, the less interconnect bandwidth is required, which matters for chip and system design economics.
insights.quote: the bandwidth requirement of a communications channel is inversely proportional to the intelligencer at either end of the channel linking two compute devices

insights.claim: Jim Handy predicts AI will eventually become embedded at all endpoints and within the communication channel itself, to the point where it becomes effectively invisible as a discrete layer.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A long-horizon vision that AI compute diffuses into infrastructure (memory, interconnect, microcontrollers) rather than remaining concentrated in discrete accelerator chips — relevant to how far 'AI hardware' investment theses should extend beyond GPUs/HBM.
insights.quote: I'm expecting to see AI permeate everywhere... I'm expecting to see it in the communication channel, and it will get to the point where it's invisible.
